description:
Fire behaves differently in microgravity. Sensors built for buildings and planes weren't designed for it. NASA has decades of microgravity combustion data, but it's scattered. We're turning it into insights that inform how we detect and respond to fire risk in space.

Main Tech: Agentic AI, RAGs, Hardware, LLMs, Sensor Fusion
summary:
We noticed that in microgravity, smoke does not rise. Airflow is what can continue to feeds a fire, which makes ceiling smoke detectors useless in space. Pyron turns NASA's own microgravity combustion research into fire safety that acts on this.

Our dashboard puts NASA data to work. It brings 129 BASS-II experiment records into a searchable explorer and lets crews ask plain-language questions, answered from NASA documents with page citations. Its key finding is that flames starve when airflow stops, and the dashboard turns that into a safety rule.

The Pyron Node runs that rule on the device. It's an ESP32 with an MQ-2 gas sensor and two servo dampers in a small habitat module. When it detects fire gases, it decides locally and closes both vents to cut the airflow, the same first response the ISS uses. It streams live readings to Mission Control, and a comparison mode that keeps vents open, as on Earth, shows why that instinct fails in space.

Future Moon and Mars crews will be far from help. Fire safety there has to match how fire actually behaves, and decades of NASA research should drive it.
details:
Pyron turns NASA microgravity fire research into a working safety rule for a spacecraft habitat. On the ISS, the BASS-II experiment burned real material samples at controlled airflow. When the airflow stopped, the flames starved and went out. Pyron automatically applies that finding.

The Pyron Node (Physical AI) is an ESP32-S3 inside a cardboard habitat model. It has an MQ-2 gas sensor and two servo dampers on the inlet and outlet vents. When the sensor picks up combustible vapor, the board closes both vents within about 2 seconds to cut the airflow a fire needs. Then it reopens once the hazard clears. The decision runs on the board, so it keeps working if the laptop link drops.

A FastAPI dashboard with a RAG layer over NASA combustion papers explains why the rule works. It shows live sensor data and lets you switch between NASA mode (close the vents, starve the flame) and Earth mode (keep the vents open, since on Earth closing them doesn’t help).

Tools: MicroPython, Python, FastAPI, pyserial, Thonny, an ESP32-S3, an MQ-2 sensor, SG90 servos and a bench power supply. We tested with hand sanitizer vapor instead of open flame for safety. We tuned thresholds from measured sensor data and kept the hardware cheap so it could be built anywhere.

What makes it creative: We are using a software + physical AI hardware solution it treats airflow as the fire suppressant instead of chemicals. That only works in microgravity and it’s what the NASA data shows.
